title: How to Pick the Right Crate Size Without Guessing
description: A crate that's too big lets a dog use one end as a bathroom, while one that's too small is genuinely uncomfortable. Here's how to measure your dog correctly instead of guessing based on breed size charts.
quick_answer: The right crate size lets your dog stand up fully without ducking, turn around completely, and lie down stretched out without touching either end. Measure your dog's height from the floor to the top of their head while standing, and their length from nose to base of tail, then add a few inches to each for a comfortable fit. Breed-based size charts are a rough starting point at best, since dogs of the same breed can vary a lot in actual size.
card_summary: Breed charts are a guess. Measuring your actual dog isn't.

faqs.question: Is it bad if a crate is too big?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially for crate training. A crate with too much extra space lets a dog use one end as a bathroom while still sleeping comfortably at the other end, which works against the instinct crate training relies on, that dogs generally don't want to soil the space they sleep in.

faqs.question: Should I size a crate for my puppy's adult size or their current size?
faqs.answer: Size for their current size, using a divider panel if the crate is designed for one, so the usable space grows as your puppy does. Buying a crate that's already adult-sized for a puppy creates the same too-much-space problem as buying any crate too large.

faqs.question: How much extra room should I add to my dog's measurements?
faqs.answer: A few inches in both height and length is usually enough for comfortable movement without leaving so much extra space that the crate stops feeling like a den. Significantly more than that starts working against the purpose of a properly sized crate.

faqs.question: Do breed size charts ever work for picking a crate?
faqs.answer: They can work as a rough starting point, but actual size varies enough within breeds that they shouldn't replace measuring your specific dog. Two dogs of the same breed can have meaningfully different crate-fit needs.

body:
## Why are breed size charts not reliable enough on their own?

Because individual dogs vary more than breed averages suggest.

A breed chart gives you a general size range, but two dogs of the same breed can differ enough in actual height and length that one fits comfortably in a given crate size while the other doesn't. Breed charts are a reasonable starting point for narrowing down options, not a substitute for measuring your specific dog.

## How do I actually measure my dog for a crate?

Two measurements matter most.

**Height:** Measure from the floor to the top of your dog's head while they're standing naturally, not stretching up. This tells you the minimum interior height your dog needs to stand without ducking.

**Length:** Measure from the tip of your dog's nose to the base of their tail, not including the tail itself. This tells you how much length your dog needs to lie down fully stretched out.

Once you have both measurements, add a few inches to each. That gives your dog room to comfortably stand, turn around, and stretch out without the crate being so oversized that it stops functioning like a den.

## Why does a few extra inches matter, but not a lot more?

Because too much space works against the actual purpose of a crate.

A small amount of extra room keeps the crate comfortable. A large amount of extra room gives your dog enough space to use one end as a bathroom while still sleeping comfortably at the other end, which undermines crate training, since it relies partly on most dogs not wanting to soil the space where they sleep.

The goal isn't the smallest crate that technically fits, it's a crate sized closely enough to feel like an actual den, not a small room.

## What if I have a puppy that's still growing?

Size for their current measurements, not their projected adult size, and use a divider panel if the crate includes one.

A divider lets you start with a smaller usable space appropriate for your puppy's current size, then expand that space in stages as they grow, instead of buying multiple crates or starting with a crate that's already too large for a young puppy to use effectively.

## Does crate shape matter as much as size?

Size matters more, but shape affects how that size actually feels. A crate that's technically tall enough but very narrow can still feel cramped for turning around, even if the height and length measurements check out individually. Make sure the width gives your dog enough room to turn around comfortably, not just stand and lie down.

## What if my dog seems anxious in a correctly sized crate?

Sizing isn't the only factor in crate comfort. A correctly sized crate that's placed in a high-traffic, noisy area, or introduced too quickly without positive association, can still cause anxiety regardless of fit. If sizing seems right but your dog is still uncomfortable, the issue is more likely about placement, introduction, or training pace than the crate's dimensions.

## The bottom line

Guessing based on breed alone leaves real room for error. Measuring your actual dog's height and length, then adding a modest buffer, gets you a crate sized for comfort without tipping into too much space.
